intoxication, while he, Schelling, enjoys the best of health, and Fichte could only have learned of any such thing from his own servant. He accuses him of having abandoned knowledge and preached instead not-comprehending and faith. He sees in him a rhetorician who can write orthographically, form periods, and rival Nicolai — who was actually Fichte's fiercest opponent — in clarity of shallow comprehensibility. Fichte as oxygen and Nicolai as hydrogen, united, would give the true water of the age. He defends the enthusiasts against him and says on p. 156: "When I recall the many soulful and heartfelt utterances of our Leibniz, Kepler, and many others — all of which, according to Mr. Fichte, would have to be considered nonsense — I cannot help but consider that he has shown himself to be the most spiritless and heartless of all philosophers who have made a name for themselves." He even accuses him — which seems to me the strongest charge against Fichte — of cowardly cleverness. He remained, he says, obligated to the proof that Schelling had misunderstood him. P. [ ]: "It remained at silence, which at the same time afforded several advantages. It spared the trouble of setting against the allegedly misunderstood system the correctly understood one, which would remove all misinterpretations — with which one risked, at the present time, only entangling oneself further and talking oneself in deeper. There might indeed here and there still be some good-natured soul who interpreted the silence as noble contempt (although otherwise no opponent seemed too lowly for Mr. Fichte to instruct); or as a fruitful and pregnant lull before a storm, of which one could not possibly foresee that it would dissolve into as gentle a rain as it now has in the Blessed Life." P. 163: "I call upon every honest man and thinker to say whether Mr. Fichte's attack on natural philosophy was not conducted behind his opponent's back and by stealth, such that the latter must still turn around, face the following crowd, and say: it is I whom he has wounded. We have stood against him in honest, open combat, with scientific weapons and in scientific form, before the eyes of the thinking men of our nation. He carries out his blows against us before Berlin ladies, privy councillors, merchants, and the like; in the dark of a private lecture he scatters slanders against those who cannot defend themselves, until

Schelling malte dagegen mit ironischer Färbung aus, wie er, weil er das Ungdttliche in seiner Nichtigkeit begriffen, von einer Zeit gehaßt und verfolgt werden mußte, die, was Fichte in den Grundzügen gesagt hatte, das Zeitalter der absoluten Sündhaftigkeit sei S. 149: „die Erscheinung einer Lehre, welche alle Existenz des Ungötrlichen leugnet in einem Zeitalter, dessen Moral auf eben dieser Existenz beruht, muß nothwendig, in diesem Zeitalter selbst, ganz eigne mo: ralische Wirkungen hervorbringen, über die sich nur der Unwissende wundern kann. Hätten wir etwa Recht in dem, was wir von der Moral der Zeit sagen, wenn unsere Lehre nicht auf die unsittlichste Weise aus Gründen der Sittlichkeit – von Menschen, die gegen uns selber den höchsten Mangel an Sittlichkeit bekämpft beweisen zur Ehre ihrer Sittenlehre würde? Was haben wir denn selbst, ale die beiden Pole des Bebens gesetzt?

Schelling, by contrast, depicted with an ironic tinge how he, because he had grasped the ungodly in its nullity, necessarily had to be hated and persecuted by an age which — as Fichte had said in the Characteristics — is the age of absolute sinfulness. P. 149: "The appearance of a doctrine which denies all existence of the ungodly, in an age whose morality rests on precisely this existence, must necessarily produce, within that age itself, quite peculiar moral effects, at which only the ignorant can be surprised. Would we be right in what we say of the morality of the age, if our doctrine were not combated in the most immoral way, on grounds of morality, by people who display toward us themselves the greatest lack of morality — for the honor of their moral doctrine? What have we ourselves posited as the two poles of life?

Die heilige Sitte von der einen; die religiöse Begeisterung von der andern Seite. Eben diese aber sind, ausgestorben und Bertilgt in der herrschenden Lehre und Biloung, „und an ihre Stelle ist etwas getreten, das von beiden nichts enthält, und beide von sich ausschließt.

Sacred custom on the one side, religious enthusiasm on the other. But these very things have died out and been extinguished in the prevailing doctrine and culture, and in their place has stepped something that contains neither of the two, and excludes both from itself.

p. 281

Kann es uns nun wundern, daß uns're fehse an sich zunddst die Verwildes [p. 281] rung der Zeit empfindet, und muß sie nicht die Folgen derselben ruhig tragen und als eben so viele Beweise von der Wahrheit dessen aufnehmen, was sie von der Beschaffenheit der jeßigen Moral behauptet? Kann ich - selbst mich wundern darüber „daß ich nun schon lange Zeit hier und das noch mit Gründen bestritten werde, altgemein aber ein Ziel der lüge, der Bosheit und der persönlichen Verfolgung geworden bin? Habe ich das nicht Alles reichlich verdient? Habe ich nicht den Schlechten, und Geistlosen, nach Gelegenheit und Umständen, viel Böses gethar ,'. der Pharifáer und Heuchler nicht geschont, manchem derselben das Schafbe kleid ausgezogen und die innere Lüde entlarvt? So bin ich auch von jeher der Empfindetei aller Art herzlich gram gewesen und habe dadurch mein -b8fe8 Herz deutlich genug vewrathen. Hätte ich auf Grund: fáße der Ehre gerechnet, so gefchabe mir doppelt Recht: denn ich mußte já wissen, daß die innere Ehrlosigkeit sich selbst, ohne Inebre zu fürchten, bekennt, und daß ihr nichts geschadet wird, wenn sie als solche hingestellt wird. Der Mensch, dem mein Ohr und meine Thür verschlossen ist, kann doch hingeben und mich of: fentlid verläumden; und er kann wissen, daß id es weiß, ohne daß er doch nöthig -bat vor mir zu er: röthen.“

Can it then surprise us that our doctrine feels first of all the wildness of the age directed against it, and must it not calmly bear the consequences thereof and accept them as just so many proofs of the truth of what it asserts about the character of present-day morality? Can I myself be surprised that I have now for a long time here and there still been opposed with arguments, but in general have become a target of lies, malice, and personal persecution? Have I not richly deserved all this? Have I not, according to occasion and circumstance, done much ill to the base and spiritless, not spared Pharisees and hypocrites, stripped the sheep's clothing from many of them and unmasked their inner deceit? So too have I always been heartily averse to sentimentality of every kind, and have thereby betrayed my wicked heart clearly enough. Had I counted on principles of honor, I would be doubly served right: for I ought indeed to have known that inner dishonor confesses itself without fear of disgrace, and that nothing harms it when it is exposed as such. The man to whom my ear and my door are closed can nonetheless go about and slander me publicly; and he can know that I know it, without having any need to blush before me."

p. 282

Gegen das Ende hin: erhebt Schelling seinen [p. 282] prophetischen Ton; die neue Erkenntnißart wird ver: kündet; das Aufhören aller Geschiedenheit der Sdu: len und Meinungen; die Schwärmer werden gelobt; er verspricht ihre Schriften zu studiren; nicht aus Berachtung, sondern aus tabelnswerther Nachlässigkeit habe er dies bisher verabsáumt.

Toward the end Schelling raises his prophetic tone; the new mode of knowledge is proclaimed; the cessation of all division of schools and opinions; the enthusiasts are praised; he promises to study their writings, having neglected this until now not out of contempt but out of blameworthy negligence.

Es werden auch ei: nige Ansáße gemacht, den reßigen Fichte von dem früheren zu untersceiden, aber der Gedanke, daß derselbe die Ideen der Naturphilosophie über Gott, Religion und Sittlichkeit an sich bringen wolle, tritt der Friedensunterhandlung immer zu störend ents gegen. Dieses Processiren über das Mein und Dein ist einmal ein Grundzug bei Schelling. S. 99 be: bauptet er auch, daß Fichte die Deutung des Fd als das logos aus seiner, Schelling's, Schrift: Philoso: phie und Religion S. 41 entlehnt habe. . Dies kann nicht hindern, zu vermuthen, daß aus Schelling Fichte nicht bloß von der Periode der Wissenschaftslehre der, sondern auch aus eben der von ihm bekämpften Per riode Manches verdanke.

Some attempts are also made to distinguish the present Fichte from the earlier one, but the thought that this same Fichte wishes to appropriate the ideas of natural philosophy concerning God, religion, and morality always intrudes too disruptively upon the peace negotiations. This litigating over "mine" and "thine" is indeed a basic trait in Schelling. On p. 99 he also claims that Fichte borrowed the interpretation of the I as the Logos from his own, Schelling's, work Philosophy and Religion, p. 41. This cannot prevent one from suspecting that Schelling too owes much to Fichte — not only from the period of the Wissenschaftslehre, but also from precisely the period he was now combating.

Schelling war indessen in München Vorstand der Akademie der fünfte und Mitglied der Akademie der Wissenschaften geworden. In einer öffentlichen Versammlung der letzteren am 12. Schelling had meanwhile become director of the Academy of Arts and a member of the Academy of Sciences in Munich. At a public assembly of the latter on October 12, 1807, on the occasion of the name-day festival of His Royal Majesty of Bavaria, he delivered an address: On the Relation of the Plastic Arts to Nature. This address is, stylistically, the most perfect thing that has flowed from Schelling's pen. One can read it again and again without ever tiring of it. Such beauty of form, however, is never possible without an adequate soundness of content.

presence of errors and other deficiencies of insight. But we must guard against letting our insight into these spoil the enjoyment of what is genuinely excellent — as so easily happens with narrow-minded people, who graze on the self-feeling of their superiority in uttering blame, and who, to keep this titillation alive in themselves, generally prefer to blame rather than to praise. And just as little as we have let polemic rest in our critique, just as little do we wish to deny apology its due, and we gladly recognize this address as a genuine masterpiece. Its title, admittedly, is poorly chosen. It should read: Some Ideas on Nature and Art.

Denn von der bildenden Kunst ist wenig die Rede, '. Wer etwa erwartet zu erfahren, wie die Architektur, Sculptur und Malerei zur Natur fido verhalte, irrt sich. Es wird von der Kunst ganz im Allgemeinen gehandelt und es sind eigentlich drei Puncte, welche Schelling abhandelt:

For there is little talk of the plastic arts as such. Whoever expects to learn how architecture, sculpture, and painting relate to nature will be disappointed. Art is treated quite generally, and there are really three points that Schelling discusses:

1) das Verhältniß der Kunst zur Natur als einer Nachahmung der Teşteren durch die erstere; 2) das Verhältniß des Foeálischen zum Charakteristischen;

1) the relation of art to nature as an imitation of the latter by the former; 2) the relation of the ideal to the characteristic;

3) "die Stufenfolge der strengen, anmuthigen und seelenvollen Form in der Entwicklung der Natur und funft.

[p. 285] Diese Probleme waren seit Lessing's Laokoon und Winkelmann's Geschichte der Kunst vielfach ventilirt worden. Göthe hatte in den Propyläen viel zur Berichtigung dieser Begriffe zu wirken gesucht und in seiner Biographie Winkelmanns 1805 war ein gewisser Abidluß der ganzen Bewegung eingetreten, dessen Ruhe auch Schellinge Abhandlung durchdringt.

These problems had been much debated since Lessing's Laocoön and Winckelmann's History of Art. Goethe, in the Propyläen, had sought to do much to correct these concepts, and in his 1805 biography of Winckelmann a certain conclusion of the whole movement had been reached, whose calm also pervades Schelling's treatise.

p. 286

Schelling bestimmte das erstere Verhältniß so, daß nicht die todte Reproduction. der Natur das Wesen der Kunst sein. könne, sondern das Produciren der Idee, welche in der Natur sich darstelle. Und eben To sei ein blos ' mechanisches Gleichgewicht kei: netwegs das Ideal der Kunst, sondern die maaßvolle Bändigung des lebenpollen Dranges, gleich wie im Sittlichen nicht die bloße Abwesenheit der Seiten: schaften den vollkommenen Charakter bilde, sondern die weise Beherrschung der Begierden und Neigungen. Die Natur aber wie die Kunst zeigten in ihrer Ge: schichte eben den Fortgang von der Einbildung des gährenden - Inhalts in die Strenge der Form, bis er zulegt in der vollkommenen Einheit mit derselben durch und durch die Seele ausfirable. In dieser. Partie kommen die herrlichsten Schilderungen vor z. B. : . „In Natur und Kunst .strebt das Wesen zuerst nach der Verwirklichung, oder. Darstellung seiner selbst im Ein: zelnen [p. 286] Form in den Anfängen beider: denn ohne Begren: zung könnte das Grenzenlose nicht - erscheinen; wäre nicht Harte, so konnte Milde nicht sein, und soll die Einheit fühlbar werden, so kann dies nur durch Eigen: heit ,- Absonderung und Widerstreit geschehen. Im Des ginn daher erscheint der schaffende Geist ganz verlo: ren -in die Form, unzugänglich, verschlossen und selbst im Großen noch herb. Je mehr es ihm aber gelingt, seine ganze Fülle in Einem Geschöpf zu véreinigen: desto mehr läßt er allmählig von feiner. Strenge nach, und wo er die Form völlig ausgebildet, so daß er in ihr -befriedigt ruht, und sich selbst faßt, werheitert er sich gleichsam, und fängt an in sanften Linien sich zu bewegen. Dieses ist der Zustand der schönsten Reife und Blüthe, wo das reine Gefäß vollendet da steht, der Naturgeist frei wird von seinen Banden, und seine Verwandtschaft mit der Seele * empfindet. Wie durch eine linde Morgentöthe, die über der gan: zen Gestalt aufsteigt, fündigt sich die kommende Seele an: noch ist sie nicht dä, aber alles bereitet sich durch das leise Spiel zarter Bewegungen zu ihrem Empfange. Die starren Umrisse schmelzen und mil: dern sich in sanfte. Ein liebliches Besen, - daß weter sinnlich noch geistig, sondern umfaßlich ist. verbreitet sich über die Gestalt, und schmiegt sich allen Umrissen jeder Schwingung der Gliedmaaßen an. Dieses, wie [p. 287] gesagt, nicht greifliche und doch Allen empfindbare Wesen ist es, was die Sprache der Griechen mit dem Namen der Chariß, die unsrige als Ahmuth be: zeichnet.“

Schelling determined the first relation such that not the dead reproduction of nature can be the essence of art, but rather the producing of the Idea that presents itself in nature. And likewise a merely mechanical equilibrium is by no means the ideal of art, but rather the measured taming of the life-filled urge — just as, in ethical matters, it is not the mere absence of passions that constitutes perfect character, but the wise mastery of desires and inclinations. Nature, like art, showed in its history precisely this progress from the shaping of the fermenting content into the severity of form, until at last, in perfect unity with it, the soul radiates through and through. In this section the most splendid depictions occur, for example: "In nature and art, essence strives first for the realization, or presentation, of itself in the particular. Hence the greatest severity of form shows itself in the beginnings of both: for without limitation the limitless could not appear; were there no hardness, mildness could not be, and if unity is to become perceptible, this can happen only through particularity, separation, and conflict. At the beginning, therefore, the creative spirit appears wholly lost in form, inaccessible, closed off, and even in greatness still harsh. But the more it succeeds in uniting its whole fullness in a single creature, the more it gradually relaxes its severity, and once it has fully developed the form, so that it rests satisfied within it and grasps itself — it becomes, as it were, cheered, and begins to move in gentle lines. This is the state of the most beautiful ripeness and bloom, where the pure vessel stands complete, the nature-spirit becomes free of its bonds, and feels its kinship with the soul. As through a gentle dawn-glow rising over the whole form, the coming soul announces itself: it is not yet there, but everything prepares itself, through the quiet play of delicate movements, for its reception. The rigid outlines melt and soften into gentle ones. A lovely being, neither sensuous nor spiritual but ungraspable, spreads itself over the form, and nestles into every contour of every movement of the limbs. This — as said, ungraspable yet felt by all — is what the language of the Greeks designates by the name Charis, and ours as grace."

Gegen das Ende der Abhandlung spricht Schel: ling ein wenig von dem Unterschied der Plastik und Malerei und will an der Geschichte der Italienischen Malerei ein Beispiel seiner Theorie des Entwickelungs ganges der Kunst geben, wobei ihm Winkelmann's Unterscheidung des strengen, hohen und reizenden Style als Muster diente.

Toward the end of the treatise Schelling speaks a little of the difference between sculpture and painting, and wishes to give, from the history of Italian painting, an example of his theory of the developmental course of art, taking Winckelmann's distinction of the severe, the high, and the pleasing style as his model.

Hierbei entschuldigt sich Schelling, daß dies zwar nicht ganz der Zeit, aber doch der That nach so sich verhalten habe, will aber in der vierten Anmerkung die. Aber darin ist sie eß, daß sie die Seele, wie er sich ausdrückt, als eine zwar nicht bö bere, aber neue Stufe. der Kunst regen will. According to his theory, Michelangelo was to have the character of severity, Correggio and, even more, Raphael that of grace, Guido Reni that of soul. Schelling here excuses himself by saying that, while this may not correspond exactly in chronology, it does so in substance; but in the fourth note he also wants to justify the matter chronologically, because although Michelangelo painted the Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel only after Raphael's death, his style had already been born before him and alongside him. Schelling's theory is not wrong in that it separates the severe style from the graceful one. But it is wrong in that it wants to see soul, as he puts it, as a new — though not higher — stage of art. For instead of soul he ought to have recognized the pleasing/charming as the dissolution

Issung der erreichten idealischen Sobnheit erkerinen müssen. Schelling sagt ganz richtig, daß die Kunst auf ihrem Gipfelpuncte die früheren Momente, na: türlid als bloße Bildungsmomente, wieder durchlaufe. Eben so aber ist es nothwendig, daß die Kunst, nach: dem sie ihren Gipfel erreicht bat, in dem Fortschritt, der die Geschichte ihres Unterganges einleitet, diesel: den Momente, jedoch in einer umgekehrten Mo: dification darstellt. . Das einfach Erhabene wird zum Colossalen; die Grazie fängt an.coquett zu wer: den; die naive Nothwendigkeit der Erschöpfung eines Vorwurfs wird zur Berechnung und Anbäufung der verschiedenen Möglichkeiten, die er der verständigen Beziehung darbietet. Und so .mußte denn Schelling's Beispiel auch unzureichend werden. Correggio liebt, wie gerade seine berühmtesten Werke, seine Jo,. Antiope, Leda, zeigen, ungewöhnliche Stellungen, aber liebliche, sanftschwel: lende, jüße Formen, dámmerungslüchtige Beleuchtun: gen. Titian wird gewöhnlich viel zu einsei: tig nach seinen Venusbildern und etwa noch nach seis nem- Christo della moneta in Dresden, beurtheilt. Wer aber die Bilder aus der Leidensgeschichte von ihm im Belvedere gesehen hat, der wird wissen, welch ' einer Tiefe des Gemüths in den höchsten Sphären Rosenkranz Schelling.

back down of the ideal beauty that had been attained. Schelling says quite correctly that art, at its summit, runs back through the earlier moments — naturally as mere moments of formation. But it is just as necessary that art, after reaching its summit, in the further progress that inaugurates the history of its decline, presents these same moments, but in an inverted modification. The simply sublime becomes the colossal; grace begins to become coquettish; the naive necessity of exhausting a subject becomes the calculation and accumulation of the various possibilities it offers to the understanding relation. And so Schelling's example was bound to prove inadequate as well. Instead of Michelangelo he ought to have looked at the earlier painters Giotto, Orcagna, Cimabue, Perugino, Fiesole — and above all, if he wanted to name one all-encompassing name, Leonardo da Vinci, whom he presents as a transitional stage from Michelangelo to Correggio. With Vinci the striving for severity, for precision of form, came to a close. With him harshness softened in every direction. Raphael, however, whom Schelling also calls a philosopher and poet — which Michelangelo, in the proper sense of the word, was in a higher degree — was not only graceful but also soulful; and, half in jest, one might cite as proof that he indeed painted, unsurpassed, the story of Psyche. Michelangelo, for his part, already went beyond the soft ideal forms; he already passed over into the athletic. Daring postures, fullness and power of the limbs, entanglement of groups, manifold contrast of figures — these attracted him. Correggio was therefore his true opposite, in whom, just as in Angelo greatness began to shade over into the colossal, grace began to shade over into a melting dissolution. Correggio loves, as precisely his most famous works — his Io, Antiope, Leda — show, unusual postures, but lovely, softly swelling, sweet forms, twilight-toned lighting. If Schelling wished to name, after these painters, one more who radiates soul in the sense of a life glowing within itself yet always held in check, he would have had to name Titian, of whom he says nothing at all. Titian is usually judged much too one-sidedly by his Venus pictures and perhaps also by his Christ of the Tribute Money in Dresden. But whoever has seen his pictures from the Passion story in the Belvedere will know to what depth of feeling, in the highest spheres, [Rosenkranz, Schelling —] 19 Schelling's Later Period

[p. 290] Titian fähig gewesen. Was ist doch Guido Reni dagegen! Schelling preist das Bild, die Apotheose Maria's in München, als ein Aeußerstes der Kunst.

Titian had been capable. What is Guido Reni next to that! Schelling praises the picture of the Apotheosis of Mary in Munich as an extreme achievement of art.

Und gewiß unter den Bildern Guido's ist es vielleicht seine größte Leistung. Darüber kann ich nicht ab: urtheilen. Sonst aber scheint mir dieser Maler, dem man das Eklektische, Akademische, Erfindungslose, im Colorit namentlich Unsichere, bei aller Feinbeit der Composition, schon so sehr abmerkt und der auf mich in der Malerei gerade denselben Eindruck gemacht bat, ' wie unter den Römischen Dichtern Claudianus im Raub der Proserpina, das Prádicat der Seele gar nicht zu verdienen. Verständig ist er und sentimental. Schelling rühmt an seinen Fleisætönen die Zartheit und erinnert dabei an den Italienischen Ausdruck morbidezza. Insofern damit eine idealische Durchfich: tigkeit des Fleisches ausgedrückt sein soll, kommt dies selbe bei Correggio (außerdem bei Murillo) in ganz anderer, wahrhafter Weise vor.

And certainly, among Guido's pictures, it is perhaps his greatest accomplishment. On that I cannot pass judgment. Otherwise, however, this painter — in whom one already notices so strongly the eclectic, the academic, the lack of invention, and, for all the refinement of his composition, a particular unsureness of coloring, and who has made on me, in painting, exactly the same impression as Claudian, among the Roman poets, in the Rape of Proserpina — seems to me not to deserve the predicate of "soul" at all. He is intelligent and sentimental. Schelling praises the delicacy of his flesh-tones and recalls in this connection the Italian expression morbidezza. Insofar as this is meant to express an ideal translucency of the flesh, this same quality occurs in Correggio (and also in Murillo) in a quite different, genuine way. In Guido Reni the tints often already shade over into the sickly, the greenish, just as Rubens likes to apply such tones to the possessed.
